topics.achievement_standard_text: They conduct statistical investigations and explain the implications of obtaining data through sampling.

concept_card.core_rule: Different data collection methods have different costs, benefits and biases; a good investigation chooses a method that suits the question and population.

hint_levels.template: Identify the population before choosing a method.
Ask whether a census is practical or whether a sample is enough.
Look for who is included, who is excluded and how that could bias the data.

worked_example.question: A school wants to survey its 1200 students about canteen food quality. Explain why a census is impractical and design a stratified sampling plan by year level.
worked_example.answer: Stratified sample proportional to year level enrolment
worked_example.explanation: Stratified sampling ensures each subgroup is proportionally represented, giving more reliable results than a simple random sample.

steps.result: Surveying all 1200 students is time-consuming and costly. A representative sample gives reliable results more efficiently.
Use year levels as strata. E.g. Year 7: 200, Year 8: 180, Year 9: 220, Year 10: 300, Year 11: 160, Year 12: 140.
For a sample of 120: Year 7 $= \frac{200}{1200} \times 120 = 20$, Year 8 $= 18$, Year 9 $= 22$, Year 10 $= 30$, Year 11 $= 16$, Year 12 $= 14$.

learning_objectives: Distinguish census, sample, experiment and observation.
Explain practical implications of different data collection methods.
Identify possible sampling bias and limitations.

explanation_sections.heading: Data collection methods
explanation_sections.body: This topic is about planning reliable data collection. The method affects what conclusions can be drawn from the data.

explanation_sections.heading: Choosing a data-collection method
explanation_sections.body: Define the question and population, compare possible methods, identify practical constraints and bias risks, then choose the method that best fits the purpose.

explanation_sections.heading: Evaluating sampling plans
explanation_sections.body: Evaluate two different sampling plans for the same question and decide which produces more trustworthy evidence.

key_vocabulary.definition: The whole group being studied.
A smaller group selected from the population.
A data collection method that gathers data from every member of the population.
A systematic problem that makes data unrepresentative.

common_mistakes: Surveying the easiest people and calling it random.
Not defining the population clearly.
Assuming a larger sample fixes a biased sampling method.
real_world_connections: School surveys, health studies, elections, customer feedback and environmental monitoring.
Questioning whether data claims are trustworthy.

additional_worked_examples.question: A researcher surveys people at a shopping centre between 10 am and 12 pm on a Tuesday. Identify the type of sampling used and explain two sources of bias.
additional_worked_examples.answer: Convenience sampling — biased toward unemployed, retirees, and shoppers

steps.result: This is convenience sampling — the researcher selects whoever is available and willing.
Tuesday morning excludes full-time workers and students. Over-represents retirees, shift workers, and stay-at-home parents.
A shopping centre excludes people who shop online, live in other areas, or cannot access the centre. Results do not represent the broader population.

additional_worked_examples.question: A teacher wants to find the average homework time for Year 8 students. She asks the 5 students sitting closest to her desk. Evaluate this sampling method and suggest an improvement.
additional_worked_examples.answer: Convenience sample — biased. Use systematic or stratified sampling instead

steps.result: Selecting the closest 5 students is convenience sampling. These students may have similar homework habits (e.g. they sit at the front because they are diligent).
5 students is too small to represent the whole class reliably.
Use systematic sampling: select every 4th student from the roll, or survey the entire class (a census) if the class is small enough.

success_criteria: I can choose between a census, sample, experiment and observation for a data question.
I can identify bias, ethical issues and practical limitations in a data-collection method.

guided_practice.question: Guided: Choose census or sample: finding the opinion of all Year 8 students at a school with 240 students.
guided_practice.answer: A sample is practical; a census is possible but more time-consuming.

steps.result: All Year 8 students at the school.
A fair sample can be quicker while still informative.

independent_practice.question: Independent: To study student concentration, compare collecting data by a controlled experiment with collecting it by classroom observation. Give one advantage, limitation and ethical consideration for each method.
independent_practice.answer: An experiment can control conditions and test effects but may feel artificial and needs informed participation. Observation reflects normal behaviour but has confounding factors and requires privacy, consent and non-identifying records.

topics.achievement_standard_text: They conduct statistical investigations and explain the implications of obtaining data through sampling. | They analyse and describe the distribution of data.

concept_card.core_rule: A data distribution is described by its shape, centre, spread and unusual values, with attention to how the sample was selected.

hint_levels.template: Describe shape, centre, spread and outliers separately.
Check whether the sample was random, systematic, stratified or convenience-based.
Use the context to decide which summary is most meaningful.

worked_example.question: The ages (in years) of 11 people at a skate park are: 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 13, 13, 14, 14, 15, 28. Describe the shape of this distribution. Is it symmetric or skewed? What might explain the outlier?
worked_example.answer: Positively (right) skewed due to the outlier age 28
worked_example.explanation: Most values cluster at the lower end, with a tail stretching to the right (positive skew).

steps.result: Most ages are $10$–$15$ (skate park typical ages). One value ($28$) is much higher.
Positively skewed — data clusters on the left with a tail to the right. The $28$-year-old is an outlier, possibly a parent supervising.

learning_objectives: Analyse and report distributions from primary and secondary sources.
Compare random and non-random sampling methods.
Use centre, spread, shape and outliers to describe data.

explanation_sections.heading: Analysing distributions from samples
explanation_sections.body: This topic moves beyond calculating a mean. Students learn to describe what a distribution shows and how sampling choices affect interpretation.

explanation_sections.heading: Describing distribution features
explanation_sections.body: Identify the sampling method, organise the data display, describe shape, centre, spread and outliers, and write a conclusion that matches the context.

explanation_sections.heading: Comparing spread and consistency
explanation_sections.body: Compare two samples with similar centres but different spreads and explain which is more consistent.

key_vocabulary.definition: The pattern of values in a data set.
A typical or middle value, such as mean or median.
How much the data values vary.
A value that is noticeably far from the rest of the data.

common_mistakes: Reporting only the mean and ignoring spread or outliers.
Using a sample conclusion as if it proves something about the whole population.
Ignoring how the sample was selected.
real_world_connections: Sport statistics, class surveys, health data and public reports.
Reading data claims critically.

additional_worked_examples.question: Two classes have the same mean test score ($72$). Class A has scores from $68$ to $76$, while Class B has scores from $40$ to $100$. What can be concluded about centre and spread, and what cannot be concluded without the full distributions?
additional_worked_examples.answer: The classes have the same mean, but Class A has the smaller range and is less spread out by that measure. Shape, symmetry, clusters and bimodality cannot be determined from only the mean and range.

steps.result: Both classes have mean $72$, so their centres are equal by this measure.
Class A has range $8$ and Class B has range $60$, so Class A is less spread out by the range.
Mean and range do not show distribution shape. Raw data or a suitable display is needed before describing symmetry, skew, clusters or modes.

additional_worked_examples.question: The histogram of daily temperatures in a Queensland town shows most values between $22^{\circ}$C and $28^{\circ}$C, with a few days above $35^{\circ}$C. Describe the shape and explain whether mean or median better represents typical temperature.
additional_worked_examples.answer: Positively skewed; median is more representative

steps.result: Positively skewed — most temperatures cluster in the $22$–$28^{\circ}$C range with a right tail for hot days above $35^{\circ}$C.
The hot days (outliers) pull the mean upward. The median is unaffected by extreme values and better represents the 'typical' day.
Use the median for skewed distributions, as it is a more robust measure of central tendency.

success_criteria: I can describe distributions using shape, centre, spread and outliers.
I can judge how the sampling method affects the strength and uncertainty of an inference.

guided_practice.question: Guided: A data set has one very high outlier. Which centre is often more representative: mean or median?

steps.result: A high outlier pulls the mean upward.

independent_practice.question: Independent: Sample A is $6,7,7,8,8,9$ and Sample B is $2,5,7,8,10,13$. Compare centre and spread, describe only shape features supported by these values, and explain one limit on inference to a population.
independent_practice.answer: Both medians are $7.5$, but ranges are $3$ and $11$, so B is more spread out. A clusters near the centre; B extends further at both ends. These small samples cannot support a strong population claim without knowing how they were selected.

topics.achievement_standard_text: They conduct statistical investigations and explain the implications of obtaining data through sampling. | They compare the variation in distributions of random samples of the same and different size from a given population with respect to shape, measures of central tendency and range.

concept_card.core_rule: Random samples from the same population vary; larger samples usually give more stable estimates, but uncertainty still remains.

hint_levels.template: Compare sample results with the same statistic, such as mean or proportion.
Ask whether differences could be due to sampling variation.
Larger samples reduce variation but do not guarantee a perfect match to the population.

worked_example.question: A factory produces bolts with a target length of $50$ mm. Sample 1 ($n = 10$) has mean $49.8$ mm. Sample 2 ($n = 50$) has mean $50.02$ mm. Explain the difference using sampling variation.
worked_example.answer: Larger samples produce more reliable estimates closer to the true mean
worked_example.explanation: Sampling variation means different samples give different statistics. Larger samples reduce this variation.

steps.result: Sample 1 mean ($49.8$) is $0.2$ mm below target. Sample 2 mean ($50.02$) is only $0.02$ mm from target.
Sample 2 ($n = 50$) is five times larger, so its mean is expected to be closer to the true population mean.
The difference between $49.8$ and $50.02$ is sampling variation. The larger sample gives a more reliable estimate.

learning_objectives: Compare variation in distributions and proportions from random samples.
Recognise the effect of sample size on variability.
Use simulations to explore sampling variation.

explanation_sections.heading: Sampling variation and sample size
explanation_sections.body: This topic explains why different samples can give different results even when they are drawn fairly from the same population.

explanation_sections.heading: Comparing sample variation
explanation_sections.body: Compare sample statistics, look at variation across samples, consider sample size, and describe conclusions using uncertainty language.

explanation_sections.heading: Simulation and sample-size effects
explanation_sections.body: Use repeated simulation results to estimate how often a sample statistic falls within a chosen range.

key_vocabulary.definition: Natural differences between samples drawn from the same population.
The number of observations in a sample.
A part-to-whole comparison often written as a fraction, decimal or percentage.
A repeated model of a random process used to study possible outcomes.

common_mistakes: Assuming two different sample results mean one sample must be wrong.
Thinking a larger sample always exactly matches the population.
Comparing raw counts when sample sizes differ instead of comparing proportions.
real_world_connections: Polling, quality control, biology surveys and online ratings.
Understanding uncertainty in survey results.

additional_worked_examples.question: Four students each randomly selected $20$ lollies from a bag and recorded the proportion that were red: $0.30$, $0.25$, $0.35$, $0.20$. What does this tell us? Would using $100$ lollies per sample change the results?
additional_worked_examples.answer: Sampling variation exists; larger samples would show less variation

steps.result: The proportions range from $0.20$ to $0.35$. Even with the same sample size ($n = 20$), each sample gave a different result due to random chance.
Mean proportion $= \frac{0.30 + 0.25 + 0.35 + 0.20}{4} = 0.275$. This estimates the true proportion of red lollies.
With $n = 100$, the proportions would cluster more tightly around the true value, reducing sampling variation.

additional_worked_examples.question: Two independent random polls use the same fair sampling method. A poll of $50$ voters found $62\%$ support Party A, while a poll of $2000$ found $54\%$. Which estimate is usually more stable, and what sampling condition must still be checked?
additional_worked_examples.answer: The $2000$-voter estimate is usually more stable because random sampling variation is smaller, provided the sampling method is genuinely random, representative and similarly unbiased.

steps.result: Larger samples have less sampling variation. The $n = 2000$ poll's estimate ($54\%$) is more likely to be close to the true population proportion.
The difference may reflect random sampling variation. Prefer the larger-sample estimate only after checking that both polls used fair, representative methods; a large biased sample can still mislead.

success_criteria: I can compare sample variation and explain how sample size affects variability.
I can compare proportions rather than raw counts when sample sizes differ and describe uncertainty in sample statistics.

guided_practice.question: Guided: Sample A has $12$ successes from $20$ and Sample B has $42$ from $100$. Which proportion is larger?
guided_practice.answer: Sample A: $0.60$; Sample B: $0.42$; Sample A is larger.

independent_practice.question: Independent: Simulate repeated random samples of sizes $20$ and $200$ from the same population. Compare the ranges of the sample proportions and explain what the result does and does not show.
independent_practice.answer: The size-$200$ proportions should usually cluster more tightly, showing reduced random sampling variation. This does not remove uncertainty or correct a biased sampling method.

topics.achievement_standard_text: They conduct statistical investigations and explain the implications of obtaining data through sampling.

concept_card.core_rule: A statistical investigation should ask a clear question, collect data fairly and ethically, analyse a suitable sample and report conclusions with uncertainty.

hint_levels.template: Turn the topic into a measurable statistical question.
Check consent, privacy and fairness before collecting data.
State what the sample suggests, not what it proves with certainty.

worked_example.question: Design a statistical investigation to answer: 'Do Year 8 students at our school spend more time on screens on weekends than weekdays?' Outline each stage of the investigation.
worked_example.explanation: A statistical investigation follows four stages: posing a question, collecting data, analysing data, and interpreting/reporting.

steps.result: Refine: 'Is the mean daily screen time greater on weekends than weekdays for Year 8 students at our school?'
Stratified random sample of Year 8 students (by gender). Record screen time for one typical weekday and one weekend day using a survey.
Calculate mean and median screen time for weekdays and weekends. Use a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot or histogram to compare distributions.

State findings with evidence: 'The mean weekend screen time ($4.2$ h) was greater than weekday ($2.8$ h), supporting the hypothesis. However, the sample of $30$ may not represent all Year 8 students.'

learning_objectives: Plan and conduct statistical investigations using samples.
Use ethical and fair methods to collect data.
Make and report inferences about a population while acknowledging uncertainty.

explanation_sections.heading: Planning and reporting statistical investigations
explanation_sections.body: This topic brings the statistics cycle together: question, plan, collect, analyse, conclude and communicate.

explanation_sections.heading: Planning the investigation cycle
explanation_sections.body: Define the population and question, choose a fair sample method, collect data ethically, analyse distribution features and report findings with limitations.

explanation_sections.heading: Critiquing investigation reports
explanation_sections.body: Critique an investigation report by identifying one strength, one limitation and one improvement to the sampling design.

key_vocabulary.definition: A question expecting variable data, not one fixed answer.
A conclusion about a population based on sample data.
A method that respects consent, privacy and fairness.
The recognition that sample-based conclusions may vary or be limited.

common_mistakes: Writing a question that cannot produce variable data.
Collecting private or sensitive data without considering ethics.
Making claims about everyone from a small or biased sample.
real_world_connections: School decisions, public policy, health surveys and market research.
Communicating evidence responsibly.

additional_worked_examples.question: A student reports: 'The median homework time for our class is 45 minutes, so everyone does about 45 minutes.' Identify two errors in this conclusion.
additional_worked_examples.answer: Median doesn't mean 'everyone'; ignores spread and variation

steps.result: The median is the middle value — it does not mean 'everyone'. Half the students do less than 45 minutes and half do more.
Without the range or IQR, we don't know if values are tightly clustered (40–50 min) or widely spread (10–120 min). The spread tells us how representative the median is.
'The median homework time is 45 minutes, with an IQR of 20 minutes, suggesting moderate variation among students.'

additional_worked_examples.question: After surveying 40 students, a group concludes that 80% of all students prefer online learning. Identify limitations in this inference.
additional_worked_examples.answer: Small sample from one group cannot represent the whole school

steps.result: $n = 40$ may be too small for a whole-school claim (possibly hundreds of students).
If the 40 students are from one class or year level, the sample is not representative. Preferences may vary by year level, gender, or learning style.

Use a sufficiently large stratified random sample across relevant school groups. Choose sample size for the desired precision and available resources; no fixed percentage alone guarantees a valid inference.

success_criteria: I can plan a statistical investigation with a clear question, population and sample method.
I can report conclusions using evidence, limitations, uncertainty and ethical considerations.

guided_practice.question: Guided: Improve this question: “Do you waste too much time online?”
guided_practice.answer: Use neutral wording such as “How many hours do you spend online on a school day?”

steps.result: Ask for measurable hours without judgement.

independent_practice.question: Independent: Draft a mini-report for a random sample in which $36$ of $50$ Year 8 students preferred a later school start. Include the sample result, a cautious population inference, uncertainty, one limitation and one ethical consideration.
independent_practice.answer: $72\%$ of the sample preferred a later start. This suggests support may be common in the Year 8 population, but sampling variation remains. Check whether the random sample represented all Year 8 groups; report responses anonymously and avoid claiming that exactly $72\%$ of all students agree.

concept_card.core_rule: Complementary events cover all outcomes between an event and not that event, so their probabilities add to 1.

hint_levels.template: Define the event and its complement using 'not'.
Use P(A) + P(not A) = 1.
Check that probabilities stay between 0 and 1.

worked_example.question: A bag contains $8$ red, $5$ blue, and $7$ green marbles. Find the probability of NOT selecting a red marble. Express as a fraction, decimal, and percentage.
worked_example.explanation: Use $P(\text{not } A) = 1 - P(A)$. The complement includes all outcomes that are not the event.

steps.instruction: Total marbles and probability of red.

learning_objectives: Recognise complementary events in applied contexts.
Use the sum-to-one relationship to calculate probabilities.
Interpret probability answers as fractions, decimals or percentages.

explanation_sections.heading: Complementary events and probability sums
explanation_sections.body: This topic strengthens probability reasoning by focusing on the relationship between an event and everything outside it.

explanation_sections.heading: Using the complement rule
explanation_sections.body: Name the event, name its complement, write the probability equation, solve for the unknown, and interpret the answer in context.

explanation_sections.heading: When the complement is simpler
explanation_sections.body: Use complements to solve problems where the direct event is complicated but the 'not' event is simpler.

key_vocabulary.definition: A specified outcome or set of outcomes.
All outcomes where the event does not happen.
A measure from 0 to 1 of how likely an event is.
The full set of possible outcomes.

common_mistakes: Confusing complement with an everyday opposite rather than 'not the event'.
Forgetting that probabilities cannot be less than 0 or greater than 1.
Adding overlapping events as if they were complements.
real_world_connections: Weather forecasts, risk, games, quality control and chance-based decisions.
Calculating 'at least one' probabilities more efficiently later.

additional_worked_examples.question: The probability of a bus being late on any given day is $0.15$. Over a 200-day school year, on how many days would you expect the bus to be on time?

steps.result: We expect the bus to be on time on approximately $170$ of the $200$ school days.

additional_worked_examples.question: In a class of 30 students, the probability that a randomly selected student owns a dog is $\frac{2}{3}$. The probability that a student owns a cat is $\frac{1}{5}$. What is the probability a student does NOT own a cat? Can we find how many own neither?
additional_worked_examples.answer: $P(\text{not cat}) = \frac{4}{5}$. Cannot determine 'neither' without more information

steps.result: $1 - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{4}{5}$. So $\frac{4}{5} \times 30 = 24$ students don't own a cat.

steps.instruction: Can we find 'neither dog nor cat'?
steps.result: Not directly. Some students might own both, or the events might overlap. We need $P(\text{dog and cat})$ to use the addition law.
Without knowing how many students own both pets, we cannot determine how many own neither. The events are not mutually exclusive.

success_criteria: I can identify an event and its complement and use their probabilities to sum to 1.
I can express probability as a fraction, decimal or percentage in context.

guided_practice.question: Guided: If $P(\text{rain})=0.35$, find $P(\text{not rain})$.

independent_practice.question: Independent: The probability that at least one of two alarms sounds is easier to find from the complement. If $P(\text{neither sounds})=0.06$, find $P(\text{at least one sounds})$ and explain the complement used.
independent_practice.answer: $1-0.06=0.94$. The complement of 'at least one sounds' is 'neither sounds'.

concept_card.core_rule: Two-event probability problems can be organised with tables, tree diagrams or Venn diagrams so all combinations are visible before calculating probabilities.

hint_levels.template: Choose a representation that matches the situation: table for categories, tree for stages, Venn diagram for overlapping sets.
Make sure every outcome is counted once.
Use the diagram to identify 'and', 'or' and 'not' events.

worked_example.question: In a class of 30, 18 study French, 12 study Japanese, and 5 study both. Construct a Venn diagram and find the probability that a randomly chosen student studies neither language.
worked_example.explanation: Use the Venn diagram to count students in each region, then find those outside both circles.

learning_objectives: Represent combinations of two events using diagrams and tables.
Calculate probabilities of specific outcomes from organised representations.
Distinguish intersection, union and complement in practical situations.

explanation_sections.heading: Organising two-event outcomes

additional_worked_examples.question: A two-way table shows results for 80 students: Sport only 20, Instrument only 15, Both 10, Neither 35. Among the students who play an instrument, what fraction also play a sport?

steps.result: Instrument only ($15$) + Both ($10$) $= 25$ students play an instrument.

steps.instruction: Of those, how many also play sport?
Calculate the requested fraction within the instrument group.

guided_practice.question: Guided: Choose a representation for two coin tosses and list the sample space.
guided_practice.answer: Tree diagram or table; $\{HH, HT, TH, TT\}$.

independent_practice.question: Independent: A problem records the colour selected and the result of a coin toss. Choose a table or tree to list all combinations, then explain why that representation is clearer than a Venn diagram for this task.
independent_practice.answer: A tree or two-way table systematically lists every ordered colour–toss combination. A Venn diagram is better for overlapping set membership, not sequential combinations.

concept_card.core_rule: Simulations and repeated experiments estimate probabilities; results vary in the short run but tend to stabilise over many trials.

hint_levels.template: Record the number of trials and favourable outcomes.
Compare experimental probability with theoretical probability.
Do not expect a small number of trials to match theory exactly.

worked_example.question: A coin is tossed 200 times. Heads appeared 114 times. Calculate the experimental probability of heads. Compare with the theoretical probability and explain any difference.
worked_example.explanation: Experimental probability is based on observed results. With more trials, it converges toward the theoretical probability.

steps.result: The difference ($0.07$) is due to random variation. With more tosses (e.g. 2000), the experimental probability would be closer to $0.50$.

learning_objectives: Conduct repeated chance experiments and simulations.
Calculate experimental probabilities for compound events.
Compare experimental results with theoretical expectations and describe variation.

explanation_sections.heading: Probability experiments and simulations
explanation_sections.body: This topic uses experimentation to understand probability. Digital tools make it possible to repeat chance processes many times and observe long-run patterns.

explanation_sections.heading: Running and recording simulations
explanation_sections.body: Define the event, run or simulate many trials, record outcomes, calculate relative frequency, compare with theory and describe possible reasons for variation.

explanation_sections.heading: Stability over many trials
explanation_sections.body: Investigate how increasing the number of trials changes the stability of experimental probability.

key_vocabulary.definition: Probability estimated from observed results.
Probability calculated from equally likely outcomes or a model.
The fraction of trials in which an event occurs.
A model that imitates a chance process.

common_mistakes: Assuming experimental probability must equal theoretical probability exactly.
Using too few trials and making a strong claim.
Not defining what counts as a successful outcome before simulating.
real_world_connections: Games, weather models, risk assessment, quality testing and digital simulations.
Understanding why probability claims involve variation.

additional_worked_examples.question: A dice simulation is used to model a basketball player's free throws: rolls of $1$–$4$ mean 'score', rolls of $5$–$6$ mean 'miss'. Simulate 10 shots and find the experimental probability of scoring. How does this compare to the model's theoretical probability?

steps.result: With only 10 trials, $0.80$ vs $0.667$ shows substantial variation. With many repeated trials, the experimental proportion would usually become more stable near $\frac{2}{3}$, but no particular run is guaranteed to be closer.

additional_worked_examples.question: A game spinner is claimed to have four equally likely colours. After 500 spins, red appeared 138 times. Is this result reasonably consistent with the fair-spinner model, and does it prove the spinner is fair?
additional_worked_examples.answer: The result is reasonably consistent with the fair-spinner model, but one set of trials cannot prove that the spinner is fair.

steps.instruction: Expected frequency for a fair spinner.

steps.result: Observed $= 138$, expected $= 125$. Difference $= 13$, which is $\frac{13}{125} \approx 10.4\%$ above expected.

The observed count is reasonably close to $125$, so this result does not provide strong evidence against the fair model. It does not prove fairness; repeated evidence and an agreed decision rule would be needed for a stronger conclusion.

independent_practice.question: Independent: Design a digital simulation for drawing two counters with replacement from a bag containing 3 red and 2 blue counters. Define the compound event 'two red', state its theoretical probability, and explain how you would compare results from 20 and 1000 trials.
independent_practice.answer: Simulate two independent draws with $P(R)=3/5$; $P(RR)=9/25=0.36$. Record the relative frequency of RR. The 20-trial estimate may vary widely, while 1000 trials should usually be more stable near $0.36$.
